idiom_name: interface Events { ... } + subclass overriding on/emit with keyof Events
implementation_notes: TypeScript adds a compile-time contract to the runtime channel: an Events interface maps each event name to its payload type, and a thin subclass (or wrapper) constrains on/emit/addEventListener to that map so a misspelled event name or a wrong payload is a compile error instead of a runtime surprise. At runtime nothing changes - node:events or EventTarget does the dispatch, and the type layer disappears - which is exactly the point: the event contract is documented in the type system and refactors are checked. Use it wherever events cross a module boundary.
pitfalls: Overrides must stay structurally compatible with the base EventEmitter signatures or the subclass stops being assignable.
Types vanish at runtime: payloads arriving from untyped JavaScript or JSON are still unchecked.
Removal needs the exact handler reference, so typed wrappers should also return an unsubscribe handle rather than relying on off().

variants.name: RxJS Subject/Observable
variants.idiom_name: Subject<T>.subscribe / next, with BehaviorSubject for replay
variants.implementation_notes: RxJS models the channel as a Subject, which is both observable and observer: subscribe(observer) registers a subscriber and returns a Subscription whose unsubscribe removes it, while next(value) publishes to all current subscribers. Operators (filter, map, debounceTime, share, retry) replace hand-written per-subscriber logic, and BehaviorSubject/ReplaySubject replay the latest values to late subscribers - something a bare EventEmitter cannot do. It is the right realization when consumers transform or combine the stream rather than merely react to an event.
pitfalls: A Subject is hot: subscribers that arrive after next() miss the value - use BehaviorSubject or ReplaySubject when late subscribers matter.
Subscriptions leak unless they are unsubscribed (or completed by takeUntil/scope teardown), and an error passed to the subject completes it permanently.
The whole RxJS pipeline is per-subscription work: heavy operators in a hot bus multiply cost by subscriber count.
